descriptor: A bamboo-eating tree dweller of the eastern Himalaya, with a ringed tail and no close living relatives.

range.summary: Temperate mountain forests with a dense bamboo understorey, from Nepal through India, Bhutan and northern Myanmar to southwest China.

regions.name: Western Nepal
regions.note: The western edge of the global range, in forests from Rara National Park to Dhorpatan.

regions.name: Eastern Nepal
regions.note: Bamboo forests of Taplejung, Panchthar and Ilam hold much of the Nepal population.

regions.name: Sikkim and Darjeeling
regions.note: Singalila National Park, where Darjeeling Zoo began releasing captive-bred red pandas in 2003.

regions.name: Bhutan
regions.note: Bhutan keeps some of the least fragmented red panda forest in the Himalaya.

regions.name: Arunachal Pradesh
regions.note: Arunachal Pradesh holds the largest share of red pandas in India.

regions.name: Northern Myanmar
regions.note: Kachin State forests near Hkakabo Razi, where hunting for trade is a documented threat.

regions.name: Western Sichuan
regions.note: Minshan, Qionglai, Liangshan and Xiangling mountains hold most Chinese red pandas.

regions.name: Northwest Yunnan
regions.note: The Gaoligong and Hengduan mountains of Yunnan are a second Chinese stronghold.

regions.name: Southern Gansu
regions.note: Red pandas were reported extinct in Gansu by 1999 (Wei et al.).

regions.name: Southern Shaanxi
regions.note: Red pandas were reported extinct in Shaanxi by 1999 (Wei et al.).

regions.name: Southern Qinghai
regions.note: Red pandas were reported extinct in Qinghai by 1999 (Wei et al.).

regions.name: Northern Guizhou
regions.note: Red pandas were reported extinct in Guizhou by 1999 (Wei et al.).

source.label: IUCN Red List: Ailurus fulgens (Glatston et al. 2015)

rangeHistory.note: The Chinese losses are dated to when Wei et al. reported them in 1999; the animals disappeared earlier, on undated timelines.

population.note: No global time series exists. This extrapolation from density and habitat area is the only published global total; the estimate is the midpoint of its range. Later Red List assessments put mature individuals below 10,000 and suspect a decline of up to 50% over about two decades.

threats.title: Habitat loss and fragmentation
threats.detail: Logging, farming and roads break up the bamboo forests red pandas depend on.

threats.title: Poaching and trapping
threats.detail: Red pandas are hunted for pelts and the pet trade and caught in snares set for other animals.

threats.title: Livestock and dogs
threats.detail: Grazing herds trample bamboo, and herding dogs kill red pandas and can spread canine distemper.

places.name: Singalila National Park
places.note: Ridge-top forest on the Nepal border, one of India's most reliable red panda sites.

places.name: Taplejung and Panchthar forests
places.note: Community forests where local guardians lead small-group red panda treks.

places.name: Phrumsengla National Park
places.note: Fir and bamboo forest along the high road across central Bhutan.

places.name: Labahe Nature Reserve
places.note: Sichuan reserve where wild red pandas are seen near forest trails.

sightings.tip: Spring and late autumn bring clear skies and thinner foliage. Monsoon months mean leeches, cloud and seasonal park closures, including at Singalila.

actions.title: Sponsor a forest guardian
actions.detail: Local guardians monitor red pandas and reduce threats in community forests.

actions.title: Book community-run treks
actions.detail: Ecotrips led by local guides turn living red pandas into village income.

actions.title: Never buy red panda products
actions.detail: Pelts, hats and pet red pandas all come from animals taken from the wild.

actions.title: Choose certified wood and paper
actions.detail: FSC-certified products reduce pressure on Himalayan forests.
